Mr. Meadow is a Bitcoin artist and filmmaker in India. He prices the work in sats. The site is mrmeadow.org.
He found Bitcoin in 2017 through a friend and bought some, then spent the next years on altcoins because he could not yet tell signal from noise. He designed for a friend's wallet company, spent time at Deloitte, and worked with a Polkadot India team that was training coders in Rust and chasing funding. He kept saying that path did not make sense. By 2020 the swings had made the point. He stopped the altcoin work and put the time into Bitcoin art: take the ideas in this space and make them something a person can see.
In this episode of Share Your Bitcoin Journey, Bitcoin For The Arts founder Dion Wilson talks with him about that choice. In India he watched coins get pushed by people who could issue more of them, and he treats that power to issue as the thing that breaks the money. He says the rules eased around 2020. Buying Bitcoin, he says, is no longer treated as illegal. Selling it, he says, is taxed at 30 percent, so people buy with rupees and then leave the country to spend or sell.
The pictures follow that idea. For Bitcoin Racing in the UK he made the social posts and a playing card for fans. In the Bitcoin Design community he drew a Cashu note he believes Calle has been using, and a small app that grows or wilts a plant as the price moves. His first AI film treats Bitcoin as a meteorite in 2008. A gas moves through the city, some eyes turn red, and those people are infected with sound money. After that, fiat looks like a plastic skin. He was printing 21 copies of a mech suit that arrives in 2008. Another piece turns a payment into a tennis rally, a ball struck across the net about every ten minutes. Modeotec printed one of his images on a circuit board and showed it in El Salvador and in Germany. He made a mempool picture during the Knots and Core argument about data on the chain. The line on it is about not weighing the chain down.
He found Maya Parbhoe through a Bitcoiner Jobs post. She was building a Bitcoin school in Suriname and working toward a presidential run. He designed the banners. She had them printed and hung them on the school. A wire from the United States into India was costing 11 to 12 dollars before the work was even paid. A Lightning payment does not ask which country the file came from. Clients get a page of prices in sats.
Asanoha asked him for work for a gallery in Denver, through Bitcoin Art Magazine. Another piece was headed to an auction on scarce.city. He was looking at a plebs conference in Goa, at El Salvador, and at Lugano. A short Bitcoin film was in progress. He tells people to catch the film screenings that run the day before a conference.
His note to a filmmaker who is stuck: use your voice, learn, be kind, and show proof of work. You do not have to play the politics of the old market. Be good at the work. On a swinging price, he says zoom out, learn it before you buy it, and come in with a conviction. The presses do not stop. There will only be 21 million bitcoin.

Benjamin Ella danced seventeen seasons as a soloist of the Royal Ballet. He arrived from Melbourne at fifteen on a full scholarship, graduated with a stress fracture in the navicular, and was kept by Dame Monica Mason while two titanium pins and three hard years decided whether he would dance at all.
In this episode of Share Your Bitcoin Journey, Bitcoin For The Arts founder Dion Wilson sits down with him. Two dancers, London and New York, who both ended up on the union side of the table. Benjamin talks about a family ballet school that refused government grants, a first bitcoin purchase in 2015 that he did not understand, and the COVID years when contract negotiations, The Bitcoin Standard, and a running money printer landed at the same time.
He has stepped back from "fix the money, fix the world." Bitcoin helps a lot. It is not a cure for everything. Proverbs 11:1 is how he reads a central bank: dishonest weights. He remembers Arts Council funding falling from about half the company's money to near 19 percent. He tried twice to raise Bitcoin inside the Royal Ballet. It did not land. He would rather become a donor and let the question arrive that way.
He is in a building year. A new child. Teaching. His parents' training program in fourteen countries. A church treasury he will start with his own money. A studio in London, with his wife, that he said out loud here before it existed.
Your sats go straight to Bitcoin For The Arts to fund artists.
IN THIS EPISODE: Melbourne, Carlos Acosta, and a full scholarship at fifteen. Dame Monica Mason and the injury that almost ended it. A family school that would rather struggle than take a grant. Buying a first property on the day of the operation. Fifty pounds of bitcoin in 2015, and no understanding. COVID, the union desk, and The Bitcoin Standard. Two dancers at the top of the job, and a paycheck that was still not a life. Flight Pattern, The Dante Project, and why Bitcoin is not a cure for everything. Proverbs 11 and even weights. Arts Council money, from about half to near 19 percent. Christopher Wheeldon, and a slow way into the institutions. A new child, and choreography on a long clock. A church treasury, started with his own money. Coming out as a Bitcoiner after a pseudonymous account. Two tries inside the Royal Ballet. What he would tell an eighteen-year-old dancer. What a $500 to $2,000 grant would unlock: a first piece with his wife.

content:
Bitbrand makes hand-branded Bitcoin goods the old way: steel, fire, and leather. No ink, no printer, and no two pieces alike. He invented the Bitcoin branding iron, calls himself the branding iron broker, and built the company from the back of a van.
In this episode of Share Your Bitcoin Journey, Bitcoin For The Arts founder Dion Wilson meets Bitbrand in Jersey City, after they first met at the Midwest Bitcoin Summit in Columbus. Bitbrand tells how Bitcoin saved his life, how an ATM on the Upper East Side changed what he did with his money, and how he got sober at 30 and quit the corporate job. He open-sourced the branding iron. The Lake Satoshi crew bought one and branded their own coasters. A friend in North Jersey ships the orders and gets paid in bitcoin. Bitbrand keeps the books in bitcoin, not dollars, and puts the gains back into the work.
He is heading to El Salvador with a small run of handmade hats. He talks about paying for coffee through Square, why prices going up is a currency collapse, and what a $500 to $2,000 Bitcoin For The Arts micro-grant would unlock: materials, a sales rep, and better product.
This audio leaves out the Halloween skit. The full video is on YouTube: https://youtu.be/rXqC851gJSY
